1:
Calvin begins by refusing the obvious reading of the first verse. It might have been counted among the promises by which the law was ratified; but he takes its design to be simply to attract them by the sweetness of the promised inheritance, so that the nearness of Canaan ought to make them take up God's yoke more cheerfully. What settles it is the latter clause: Moses did not merely promise a reward for keeping the law, but set before them the previous favour with which God had gratuitously prevented them, that they might show themselves grateful. Henry draws the terms of obedience from the same verse — careful, universal, and from a good principle, with a reverence of God's majesty and a dread of his wrath. Ellicott wonders whether the verse belongs at the end of the previous paragraph, and notes that possessing the land means not the first conquest so much as the detailed work left to Israel afterwards.

On the command to remember, the question is what the forty years were for, and whether the proving was for God's information or for Israel's. Keil says God desired to humble them and prove the state of their heart, humiliation being the way to prove their attitude towards him. Wesley turns it the other way: the point was that they might discover to themselves and to others the infidelity, inconstancy, hypocrisy and perverseness that lay hid in their heart, a discovery of singular use both to them and to the church in all succeeding ages. Ellicott gives the third answer, that the delay was pedagogical. It was three days' journey to Sinai and eleven days from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea, and it was in God's power to bring them up without delay at all; so too there is no necessary impossibility in the immediate turning of anyone from darkness to light — but the formation of character by probation and training would vanish in such a process. He adds that the word rendered way means the manner rather than the route, and that in all these things the Israelites were types of us. Henry keeps the same thought as a figure of schooling: the wilderness was the school in which they had been boarded and taught for forty years under tutors and governors, and now that they had come of age they must be reminded of the discipline of their minority.

The manna divides them again. Keil insists the humiliation lay not merely in hunger but in the unfamiliar food itself, and denies flatly that what proceeds out of the mouth of the Lord is the word of the law, as he says the Rabbins suppose. Ellicott notices that the manna was withheld for a whole month, until the sixteenth day of the second month, so that they were left to their own resources first; afterwards it was not withheld for thirty-nine years and eleven months. He also observes that our Lord was led forty days in the wilderness, a day for each year of the Exodus, living on the word of God. Calvin makes the lesson an attack on ordinary religious perception: men's senses are so tied to meat and drink that they rise no higher, they bind God to the outward means as though his hand could effect nothing without instruments, and the acknowledgment that the earth's fruits come from him is a cold notion which speedily vanishes. Wesley reads every word to mean anything God appoints for the purpose, however unlikely, since it is not the creature but the command and blessing upon it that sustains life; Clarke concludes that God permits no tribulation he does not mean to turn to advantage, privations being the forerunners of mercy. Gill turns the command inward, bidding believers remember how they were brought to see their wilderness condition by nature and were stopped in their career of sin.
4:
Whether the raiment that waxed not old requires a miracle is argued here at length, and the four answers cover the whole range. Clarke calls it a much-tortured text and reads it plainly: God so amply provided the necessaries of life that they were never obliged to wear tattered garments. A people who had carvers and jewellers and embroiderers for the tabernacle presumably had makers of clothes and sandals too, they traded with Moabites and wandering Arabians, and they had sheep and cattle enough to supply much of the material themselves. Then he prices the alternative. To make the clothes themselves outlast forty years would require not one miracle but a chain of the most astonishing miracles ever wrought: six hundred thousand males were born in the wilderness, so every child's garment would have to grow with him, which means a miracle continually wrought on every thread and on every particle of matter composing it, while the parent's clothes shrank to fit the child and stretched again afterwards. No such interference, he concludes, was necessary. Gill goes half the distance, rehearsing the Jewish explanations — the clothing of those who died, the spoil taken from Amalek, the stores brought out of Egypt, and the observation that manna produced no sweat, which is prejudicial to clothes — and then insists that even granting all that, it must still be miraculous that what they wore did not wear out. Keil resists the naturalising on philological grounds: the verb means to fall off through age, the word for the foot occurs only here and at Nehemiah 9:21 and is of doubtful sense, and the clause affirms something more than that clothes and shoes never failed them, against the commentators who have said so. Ellicott holds the middle: we cannot say anything miraculous is certainly intended, though it is not impossible, and providence may simply have directed them to clothe themselves suitably, as God taught them to clothe his own tabernacle with fabrics and skins.

Gill and Ellicott then arrive independently at the same application, that raiment which never wears out is the everlasting righteousness of Christ; Ellicott adds the fine linen which is the righteousness of saints, and the promise that they who wait on the Lord shall walk and not faint, observing that those appointed to enter Canaan were kept in health for the journey exactly as those appointed to die could not be.

On the chastening of a son the striking thing is a documented dependence. Calvin objects that the verb is taken by some in too restricted a sense, as though it meant only to chastise, whereas it comprehends the whole process of a proper education, so that Israel had been taught and kept under the best discipline and God had omitted nothing required of the father of a family. Keil, three centuries later and in another tradition, makes the same point on the same word, glosses it as admonish, chasten, educate — and quotes Calvin by name for the judgment that it includes everything belonging to a proper education. Ellicott takes the analogy as proof of love rather than of method: Proverbs 13:24 has the father seeking chastening for his son early, all training necessarily implies time and cannot be done in a moment, and the point of the figure is that whom the Lord loves he chastens — else why be at the pains to chasten at all? Wesley alone reads the comparison as a set of limits on God: a man chastises his son unwillingly, constrained by necessity, moderately, in judgment remembering mercy, and for reformation and not destruction. Gill draws the obligation from both sides of the chapter at once, the bounty that provided food and raiment and the affliction that was fatherly chastisement, and holds them bound to whatever God enjoined, moral, ceremonial or judicial alike.
7:
Calvin reads the whole description as an argument rather than an inventory. Moses almost sets a habitation full of wealth before their eyes so that they may worship there more cheerfully and study to repay so signal a benefit by gratitude; and the decisive detail for him is how the land is watered. Egypt is fruitful, and marvellously so, but its fruitfulness is drawn off by drains and maintained by the hand and industry of men, whereas Canaan depends on God's blessing and waits for the rain from heaven. He presses the same point out of the phrase that the land is looked upon by God from the beginning of the year to its end: Israel would be ungrateful if they did not constantly direct their regard to him, since he never ceased daily to look on them. He concedes at once that no corner of the earth is without God's blessing, the Nile itself being witness — the difference is not in the giving but in whether the receiver can mistake the gift for his own work.

Keil sets the description against the desert term by term: well-watered where the wilderness was dry, brooks and fountains and floods rising in valleys and on hills, wheat and barley and the vine and fig and pomegranate, oil and honey, a land where bread is eaten without scarceness. Ellicott agrees the description is most attractive and then turns it: it is a long time since anyone has seen Palestine in that condition, and its desolation is as much a proof of the truth of the divine word as its beauty was. He also corrects the rendering, so that the fountains and depths go forth in the valley and on the hill, the watercourse running down the mountain-side and the still pool lying below; Wesley glosses the same word as deep wells or springs or lakes.

The iron and the brass draw three separate corrections. Clarke observes that there is no such thing in nature as a brass mine, so the word should be rendered copper, brass being made from it by the addition of another mineral. Ellicott says the same in one line — brass means copper, and so in all passages — and adds that sacred history tells us of no mining operations in Palestine at all. Keil, who takes the stones to be ferruginous and reports that modern travellers confirm it, concedes the same point, that the Israelites did not carry on mining. Wesley alone avoids the difficulty by reading the verse as surface abundance rather than extraction: iron lies about in such quantity that travellers must tread on it where elsewhere they tread on stones.

Gill and Clarke supply the produce from other sources entirely. Gill notes the two harvests, barley beginning at the passover and wheat at Pentecost, and argues the plenty from what Solomon's household consumed and from the yearly grain sent to Hiram, adding that Israel exported wheat and sold it at the market of Tyre, and that the Jewish writers named the towns where the best fine flour was to be had. Clarke devotes by far the longest note in the chapter to a traveller's observations, reporting olives eaten at Joppa said to have grown on the Mount of Olives and reckoned the best in the Levant, fig trees as fine as any there, and pomegranates singled out in the list because they are used to make cooling drinks much as lemons are used in the West; he ends among the bees of Egypt and an account of their keeping that he calls very amusing.
10:
The command to bless God after eating is treated as a real duty with rules attached. Henry gives three: they must not eat or drink so much as to indispose themselves for the blessing, but rather serve God in it with more cheerfulness; they must keep no fellowship with those who when they had eaten and were full blessed false gods, as Israel itself had done before the calf; and whatever they have the comfort of, God must have the glory of. He notes that where the Saviour taught a blessing before meat, this law teaches one after it — the first our Hosannah, the second our Hallelujah — and records the usage the religious Jews built on it, a blessing said over a cup of wine and even over the smell of a flower. Ellicott quotes the Talmud to the same effect, that it is forbidden to take any enjoyment from this present world without thanksgiving and that whoever does so is a transgressor. Wesley calls the praise a debt of justice as well as of gratitude, and turns on those who profess to believe in a God from whom all their comforts come and yet grudge to own him at their meals. Calvin puts it as a question of sense rather than of law: nothing is more unreasonable than, having eaten and been filled, not to acknowledge where the food came from. Gill adds only that the liberty to eat freely stops at intemperance.

The long warning that follows is read as syntax by one and as psychology by another. Ellicott observes that from the eleventh verse to the eighteenth is a single sentence in the Hebrew, and lays out its structure — take heed lest thou forget, lest thou eat and be satisfied, and thine heart be lifted up, and thou say in thine heart, my power; and take heed that thou remember. He then calls the caution prophetic and names those in whom it came true, Hezekiah, whose heart was lifted up, with Rehoboam who forsook the law when he had strengthened himself and Uzziah whose strength was his destruction. Keil traces the same chain plainly: plenty, then houses and herds and silver, then the lifted heart, then the forgetting of Egypt, then the wealth ascribed to one's own hand.

Calvin supplies the diagnosis, and he is bleak about it. Scarcely one person in a hundred, he says, is found in whom satiety does not generate headiness; prosperity intoxicates almost all of us, so that we grow wanton against God and forget both him and ourselves; and he recalls the Song's picture of the beloved waxen fat and grown thick, who kicked. The cause he identifies is pride, which riches ordinarily puff up: examples of moderation in prosperity are rare, and as soon as men perceive themselves flourishing they begin to admire their own exaltation until they despise God himself — which is why the rich are charged not to be high-minded. The kindlier God's dealing, the meeker our submission ought to be, and the depravity of our nature hurries us the other way, so that we grow insolent under the very indulgence that should bend us. And where the danger is not immediate it is cumulative: uninterrupted prosperity gradually corrupts even the best, until they degenerate from themselves, so that a man must beware not for a day but keep watch through the whole course of his life. Gill states the paradox more briefly, that plenty induces forgetfulness of God when one would think it should do the opposite; and Ellicott sets against the goodly houses the vow of the Rechabites to dwell in tents all their days.
13:
The lifted heart is glossed with one addition that goes beyond the text. Gill says only that the heart is apt to rise when riches increase, and that the flocks multiply because the pasture is good. Wesley expands the self-congratulation into two kinds: as if thou didst receive and enjoy these things either by thy own wisdom and valour and industry, or else for thy own merit — the second of which the verse does not say, and which turns a boast about capacity into a claim about desert.

The wilderness is then described from natural history and from philology. Gill fixes it as the wilderness of Paran, reaching from Sinai to Kadesh, eleven days' journey, with nothing to be seen but dry rocks and barren mountains; he classes the scorpion as a kind of serpent, reports from Pliny that it is continually thrusting out the sting in its tail and striking with it, and cites Aristotle that of insects this alone has a large sting. Clarke keeps to the effects and describes the bite of the fiery serpents as causing a violent inflammation with unquenchable thirst, terminating in death. Ellicott attends instead to which rock is meant, distinguishing the word used of the rock in Horeb, which carries the idea of hardness, from the word used of the rock smitten at Kadesh, which is rather a cliff or height and suggests inaccessibility; he thinks the question put to the rebels in Numbers 20:10 helps the distinction, and then admits he cannot say what its purpose may be. He collects the other occurrences of the word for flint, including the psalm that alludes to this very passage.

On the manna Calvin states the thesis the whole chapter has been building toward, and states it as a rule about perception. Bread and water both failed, and the people must have perished had God not given them both preternaturally, making the hard rock run and sending bread from heaven; the trial exposed their incredulity and their intemperance together, and God's goodness showed the more clearly because he pardoned the ingratitude and relieved the need in spite of it. Had they never gone hungry, he says, the daily supply would have been received without noticing it. Hence the closing words about doing them good at their latter end, from which he draws the general lesson: we are often deprived of necessary supplies so that our senses may wake to acknowledge the help that appears in our extremity, for abundance covers the eyes with a veil and dims their sight, while deprivation purges and removes that dimness so that the benefits God gives may be more clearly seen.

Wesley reaches the same end by the opposite road. The humbling worked by keeping them in daily dependence convinces a man what an impotent and helpless creature he is, subsisting wholly on the alms of divine goodness from day to day; but then he turns the argument round — the mercies of God, duly considered, are as powerful a means of humbling as the greatest afflictions, because they increase our debts to him and manifest our dependence, and by making God great they make us little in our own eyes. The good at the latter end he takes to mean that once purged and prepared by affliction a man may enjoy the blessings with less disadvantage, made thankful by the memory of what he suffered and more cautious not to abuse what he has.
17:
Calvin identifies the boast of the seventeenth verse as the chief form of the pride he has been tracking all through the chapter: not merely that men are lifted up in various ways, but that they assume and assign to themselves what belongs to God. Nothing, he says, confines us within the bounds of humility so effectively as acknowledging grace, since it is madness and temerity to raise our crests against the one on whom we depend and to whom we owe ourselves and all we possess. He then insists on where the fault is located. To say in the heart is a Hebraism for thinking within oneself, so the remedy Moses requires is not the outward profession of the lips — in which, he remarks, there is often nothing but hypocrisy and vanity — but a settled persuasion that whatever a man holds comes from sheer beneficence. And he ties the argument back to the manna: the food of the wilderness stands as a perpetual proof that man is not sustained by bread only but by the secret power of God, which supplies the principle of life itself.

Clarke takes the counter-statement of the next verse and turns it into a series of questions with only one answer. Who among the rich and wealthy believes this saying? Who gives wisdom, understanding, skill, bodily strength and health — and without these, how is wealth to be acquired at all? Whose is providence, who gives fertility to the earth, who brings a purpose to a right issue? The proposition is therefore self-evident to him, and he draws from it the consequence the text does not state: that to God the wealthy man must account for the manner in which he has spent the riches God gave him.

Gill reads the forgetting of the last two verses in both directions, either failing to acknowledge that the mercies came from God and ascribing them to oneself, or neglecting the duty owed for them; and he presses the warning of the parallel with the nations. Israel is threatened with exactly what is being done to the seven nations before their eyes, and might righteously expect the same treatment for the same sins, idolatry above all, since the first two precepts require the worship of one God and forbid the worship of images. He notes that where the text has the voice of the Lord, the Targum reads the Word of the Lord, and takes that for Christ, the essential Word in whom the name of the Lord was and whose voice Israel was bound to obey.

Ellicott closes the chapter as he opened it, with a question about where its edges fall. The word rendered because ye would not be obedient means in return for your disobedience, and the same word stands at Deuteronomy 7:12; the use of it in those two places, he suggests, might fairly be taken to mark off everything between them as a complete section of the discourse. Having begun by wondering whether the first verse belonged to the paragraph before it, he ends by proposing that the chapter and its neighbour form one unit bounded by a repeated word — a structural argument made twice, from opposite ends, in a chapter where every other commentator is arguing about wealth.
